truth.text:
1. A prime number has exactly two distinct positive divisors.
2. Those divisors are one and the prime number itself.
3. The number one is neither prime nor composite.
4. Two is the smallest prime and the only even prime.
5. Every other even number is divisible by two.
6. Three is the smallest odd prime number.
7. Five is the only prime whose last digit is five.
8. A composite number has more than two positive divisors.
9. Four is composite because two divides it evenly.
10. Six is composite because both two and three divide it.
11. Prime numbers serve as building blocks for positive integers.
12. Every integer greater than one has at least one prime factor.
13. A prime factor is a prime that divides a number.
14. The prime factors of twelve are two and three.
15. Repeated prime factors are included when writing a prime factorization.
16. Twelve has the prime factorization two times two times three.
17. Prime factorization is unique apart from the order of factors.
18. This uniqueness is called the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
19. Division helps determine whether a number is prime.
20. A divisor leaves no remainder when dividing a number.
21. Seven is prime because only one and seven divide it.
22. Nine is composite because three divides it evenly.
23. Ten is composite because it has factors two and five.
24. Eleven is prime because no smaller prime divides it.
25. Thirteen is prime because neither two nor three divides it.
26. A number ending in zero is divisible by ten.
27. A number ending in an even digit is even.
28. An even number greater than two cannot be prime.
29. A number ending in five is divisible by five.
30. An integer's digit sum can reveal divisibility by three.
31. Fifteen is divisible by three because its digits sum to six.
32. Twenty-one is divisible by three because its digits sum to three.
33. A digit sum divisible by nine signals divisibility by nine.
34. Divisibility tests can quickly identify many composite numbers.
35. No divisibility test alone proves every remaining number prime.
36. To test primality, check possible divisors up to the square root.
37. A composite number has a factor no greater than its square root.
38. Therefore, larger possible factors need no separate primality checks.
39. To test forty-nine, checking seven reveals its compositeness.
40. Forty-nine equals seven times seven, making seven a factor.
41. To test twenty-nine, check the primes two, three, and five.
42. None divides twenty-nine, so twenty-nine is a prime number.
43. Prime numbers become less frequent among larger positive integers.
44. Nevertheless, there are infinitely many prime numbers.
45. Euclid gave a famous proof that primes never run out.
46. His proof begins by assuming a finite list of primes.
47. Multiplying that list and adding one creates a useful number.
48. No prime on the list divides the new number evenly.
49. The new number has a prime factor outside the list.
50. This contradicts the assumption that the list contained every prime.
51. Consecutive primes have no other primes between them.
52. Two and three are the only consecutive integers both prime.
53. Three and five are consecutive primes separated by two.
54. Five and seven are another pair separated by two.
55. Prime pairs separated by two are called twin primes.
56. Eleven and thirteen form a pair of twin primes.
57. Seventeen and nineteen also form a pair of twin primes.
58. It remains unknown whether infinitely many twin prime pairs exist.
59. Gaps between consecutive primes can be surprisingly large.
60. Long strings of composite numbers can occur between primes.
61. For any positive integer, factorials help construct composite strings.
62. A factorial multiplies every positive integer up to a chosen number.
63. Five factorial equals one times two times three times four times five.
64. Adding two to five factorial gives a number divisible by two.
65. Adding three to five factorial gives a number divisible by three.
66. Such constructions demonstrate arbitrarily long runs of composite numbers.
67. An odd number leaves remainder one when divided by two.
68. Every prime greater than two must therefore be odd.
69. Oddness alone does not guarantee that a number is prime.
70. Nine is odd but composite because three divides it.
71. Every prime greater than three lies beside a multiple of six.
72. Such a prime has remainder one or five upon division by six.
73. Numbers beside multiples of six are not necessarily prime.
74. Twenty-five fits that pattern but equals five times five.
75. The greatest common divisor is shared by two integers.
76. It is the largest positive integer dividing both integers.
77. The greatest common divisor of eight and twelve is four.
78. Two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is one.
79. Eight and fifteen are coprime despite both being composite.
80. Distinct prime numbers are always coprime to each other.
81. A common multiple is divisible by each specified number.
82. The least common multiple is the smallest positive common multiple.
83. The least common multiple of four and six is twelve.
84. Prime factorizations help calculate greatest common divisors efficiently.
85. Prime factorizations also help calculate least common multiples efficiently.
86. For two integers, their gcd times their lcm equals their product.
87. The Euclidean algorithm finds greatest common divisors through repeated division.
88. Each step replaces larger numbers with a smaller remainder.
89. The process ends when a division leaves zero remainder.
90. The last nonzero remainder is the greatest common divisor.
91. A remainder describes what remains after integer division.
92. Seventeen divided by five leaves a remainder of two.
93. Numbers with equal remainders can share useful arithmetic properties.
94. Modular arithmetic studies numbers according to their division remainders.
95. An even number is congruent to zero modulo two.
96. An odd number is congruent to one modulo two.
97. Ten is congruent to one modulo three.
98. Thirteen is also congruent to one modulo three.
99. Adding congruent numbers preserves the corresponding remainder relationship.
100. Multiplying congruent numbers also preserves that remainder relationship.
101. A prime divides a product only if it divides some factor.
102. This property helps establish the uniqueness of prime factorization.
103. If three divides a product, it divides at least one factor.
104. The same statement holds for every prime number.
105. Composite divisors need not satisfy that product property.
106. Six divides twelve, although six divides neither three nor four.
107. A perfect square equals an integer multiplied by itself.
108. Every exponent in a square's prime factorization is even.
109. Thirty-six is a square because six times six equals thirty-six.
110. Thirty-six factors as two squared times three squared.
111. A cube equals an integer multiplied by itself three times.
112. Every exponent in a cube's prime factorization is divisible by three.
113. Twenty-seven is three cubed and therefore a perfect cube.
114. The divisors of a prime are particularly easy to count.
115. Every prime has exactly two positive divisors by definition.
116. A square of a prime has exactly three positive divisors.
117. Twenty-five has divisors one, five, and twenty-five.
118. Counting divisors becomes easier after finding the prime factorization.
119. Each prime exponent contributes choices to a divisor.
120. Multiplying those choice counts gives the total number of divisors.
121. Twelve has six positive divisors in total.
122. Its divisors are one, two, three, four, six, and twelve.
123. A proper divisor is smaller than the number it divides.
124. Every number greater than one has one as a proper divisor.
125. The sum of proper divisors defines several number categories.
126. A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors.
127. Six is perfect because one plus two plus three equals six.
128. Twenty-eight is another perfect number from elementary number theory.
129. An abundant number exceeds the sum of its proper divisors.
130. A deficient number exceeds that sum of its proper divisors.
131. Prime numbers are deficient because one is their only proper divisor.
132. Goldbach's conjecture concerns sums of two prime numbers.
133. It proposes that every even integer above two has such a sum.
134. For example, ten equals three plus seven.
135. Twelve equals five plus seven, offering another example.
136. The conjecture remains unproved despite extensive numerical checking.
137. A Mersenne number is one less than a power of two.
138. Some Mersenne numbers are prime, while many others are composite.
139. Seven is prime and equals two cubed minus one.
140. Fifteen is composite and equals two to the fourth minus one.
141. A Fermat number is one more than a particular power of two.
142. Some small Fermat numbers are prime, but others are composite.
143. Prime numbers matter in both theoretical mathematics and practical computing.
144. Some encryption systems use arithmetic involving very large primes.
145. Finding prime factors of large numbers can require substantial computation.
146. Modern algorithms can test enormous numbers for primality.
147. A sieve finds primes by removing multiples of smaller primes.
148. The sieve of Eratosthenes is a classic example.
149. It begins with small numbers and repeatedly crosses out composites.
150. The numbers left uncrossed are prime within the chosen range.
